title: 0.5s Reflex
subtitle: Tap the instant the screen flashes
desc: A free one-button reaction test you can play in 20 seconds. The screen flashes at a random moment — tap as fast as you can. Works on phone and desktop, no install.
howto: Tap START. The screen stays dark for a random 0.8–2.5 seconds.
The moment it flashes white, tap. Your reaction time is shown in milliseconds.
Tap the green flash early and you get a foul — that round does not count.
tips: Look at the whole screen, not one spot. Peripheral vision reacts faster.
Breathe out as you wait. Holding your breath makes you flinch.
Under 200 ms is elite. The average human is around 250 ms.
body: Reflex started as a joke about how bad reaction tests look on phones: you tap, the screen flashes, and by the time you react the result is already gone. So the whole game is one frame of input — the flash is unmissable, and the only thing that matters is the gap between seeing and moving.

It is built on a shared 40 KB canvas engine and runs in a single file. There is no login, no leaderboard server, no loading bar. The random delay is real randomness, not a fixed timer, so you cannot learn the rhythm — you can only get better at waiting.

If you want to compare with friends, the result screen generates a share card with your exact milliseconds. Screenshot it, send it, and watch people immediately try to beat it — that loop is the entire reason the game exists.

title: Hold the Line
subtitle: Release in the green zone
desc: Free browser game: hold to charge a bar, release it inside the moving green zone. Ten rounds, one thumb, under a minute.
controls: Hold pointer down to charge, release to fire
howto: Press and hold anywhere to fill the bar.
A green zone slides along the bar faster each round.
Release while the fill is inside the green zone. Miss twice and the run ends.
tips: Charge past the zone and wait for it to come back — the bar is a clock.
Rounds 7–10 are about releasing on the way in, not the way out.
One clean run takes about 50 seconds, which is exactly the point.
body: Timing games usually punish you by making the target smaller. Hold the Line punishes you by making the target faster, which keeps the failure readable: you always know you were a fraction early, not that the game cheated.
The engine is the same container as every other game here — a fixed 720×720 stage that letterboxes onto any screen. Physics is `value += rate * dt`, so it behaves identically at 30 fps and 144 fps.
Misses are loud on purpose. Feedback within one frame is the difference between 'unfair' and 'my fault', and this game lives entirely on that line.

title: Pocket Coin
subtitle: A two-second coin flip you can call
desc: A third-party submission: call heads or tails, flip, and get a shareable result. Uploaded by a community creator and hosted in our standard container.
howto: Tap to flip. The coin spins once and lands.
Win streaks are tracked locally, nothing is uploaded.
tips: It is a fair coin. That is the whole joke.
body: This page is a live test of the third-party slot: it was added by editing one entry in `data/games.json` and dropping one folder into `games/`. No review queue, no manual layout, no screenshot upload — the cover is generated from the title, and the SEO page is built from the metadata.

Because it is a third-party game it gets the same container, the same anti-hijack guard and the same share card, but its author line points at the submitter instead of us. If a game is pulled for a rule violation, the build removes its pages, its embed widget and its sitemap entry in one command.
That is the entire economic argument for an open slot: supply grows without growing the review team.
